title: Ribosome
summary: The ribosome is the protein builder of the cell - a tiny two-part machine that reads a cell's instruction and links amino acids into proteins. Explore how it reads the code, joins the pieces, and why this small organelle matters in every living cell.

compareCandidate.label: Free ribosomes vs. rough-ER ribosomes
compareCandidate.description: Free-floating ribosomes build proteins the cell uses inside itself. Ribosomes clamped onto the rough ER build proteins that get packaged and shipped out to other parts of the cell or the body.

processes: Translation: reading the code to build a protein
Linking amino acids in the order given
plainLanguageExplanation: The ribosome is the tiny factory that makes proteins. It reads a copy of an instruction from the cell's DNA and, following it like a recipe, joins small building blocks called amino acids together in the exact order shown. The chain folds into a protein that does real work, like building structure, moving molecules, or fighting germs. Ribosomes can float free in the cytoplasm or clamp onto the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Either way, their one job is to read the code and build protein to match.

keyFacts.label: Main job
keyFacts.value: Builds proteins by linking amino acids in the order the code says

keyFacts.label: Size
keyFacts.value: One of the smallest but most numerous organelles in a cell

keyFacts.label: Where found
keyFacts.value: Floating free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER

keyFacts.label: How it works
keyFacts.value: Reads a messenger code, then joins amino acids to form a protein

keyFacts.label: Everywhere
keyFacts.value: Found in all living cells, from bacteria to human cells

whyItMatters: Without ribosomes, no cell could build proteins, and without proteins nothing could be made, moved, or repaired. They turn the cell's stored instructions into the actual working molecules of life.
didYouKnow: A single active cell can hold millions of ribosomes, each snapping amino acids together in under a second.
